claims.source: When these changes were introduced individually or together in the laboratory, the resulting polymerase showed greater activity in a minigenome assay, but replication was unchanged or attenuated in vitro, in mice, and in ferrets (Herfst et al., 2010; Jagger et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Herfst et al., 2010; Jagger et al., 2010

claims.claim: After the 2009 pandemic strain was identified, other sites within PB2 were identified and found to be responsible for human adaptation.
claims.source: After the pandemic strain was identified and its anomalous residues at these sites noted, other sites within PB2 were identified and found to be responsible for human adaptation (Mehle and Doudna, 2009; Yamada et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mehle and Doudna, 2009; Yamada et al., 2010

claims.claim: All three of the traits (receptor binding, pH of activation, polymerase efficiency) must be simultaneously present at least to some degree for a strain to cause a pandemic.
claims.source: Based on the evidence to date, it seems clear that all three of the traits considered in this review, and possibly others in Table 1, must be simultaneously present at least to some degree for a strain to cause a pandemic.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the analysis of pandemic viruses

claims.claim: With only a few instances of pandemic strains emerging per century, it should not be surprising that a new pandemic strain would violate an apparent rule of human adaptation that applied perfectly to previous pandemic strains.
claims.source: Yet with only a few instances of pandemic strains emerging per century, it should not be surprising that a new pandemic strain would violate an apparent rule of human adaptation that applied perfectly to previous pandemic strains, as in the case of the PB2 residues associated with human adaptation in 2009, or as in the case of activation pH of HA in early 2009 isolates (Russier et al., 2016), which had a value outside the range previously seen in human influenza viruses.
claims.evidence: Logical reasoning about rare events and supported by citation to Russier et al., 2016

claims.claim: It is unclear whether the list of sites and phenotypic traits associated with human adaptation is nearly complete or will continue to grow as we experience additional pandemics.
claims.source: It is unclear whether the list of sites and phenotypic traits associated with human adaptation is nearly complete or will continue to grow as we experience additional pandemics.
claims.evidence: Acknowledgment of uncertainty about future discoveries

claims.claim: For receptor binding and acid stability, full human adaptation may not be required to initiate a pandemic in a virus that is otherwise well-adapted for humans.
claims.source: At least for the traits of receptor binding (Childs et al., 2009) (Table 2) and acid stability (Russier et al., 2016) (Table 3), full human adaptation may not be required to initiate a pandemic in a virus that is otherwise well-adapted for humans.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Childs et al., 2009 and Russier et al., 2016 and data in Tables 2 and 3

claims.claim: Failure of a nonhuman influenza virus to fully meet the three criteria (receptor binding, pH of activation, polymerase efficiency) does not disqualify it from posing a significant risk of a pandemic.
claims.source: Thus, whether or not the list of traits required for pandemic is now complete, our understanding of where the threshold lies for being sufficiently human-adapted continues to change.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the examples of incompletely adapted pandemic viruses

claims.claim: Even a virus perfectly adapted for human-to-human transmission might fail to transmit extensively, due to ecological factors, chance, or both.
claims.source: While the biological properties of a virus certainly play a large role in determining the pandemic risk posed by a strain, it is possible that even a virus perfectly adapted for human-to-human transmission might fail to transmit extensively, due to ecological factors, chance, or both.
claims.evidence: Speculation about factors beyond viral properties

claims.claim: Initiation of a pandemic requires not only a well-adapted virus but ecological opportunity to spill over into humans.
claims.source: Initiation of a pandemic requires not only a well-adapted virus but ecological opportunity to spill over into humans (perhaps multiple times if the first introduction is not "successful" [Mills et al., 2006]), as well as a human population that is immunologically susceptible and sufficiently connected to establish ongoing transmission (Box 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mills et al., 2006 and logical reasoning

claims.claim: Selection pressures for within-host proliferation and competition may diverge from those needed for efficient transmission.
claims.source: Additional complexity arises from the fact that selection pressures for within-host proliferation and competition may diverge from those needed for efficient transmission (Park et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2013

claims.claim: Genetic bottlenecks at the time of transmission may enhance the role of chance.
claims.source: Genetic bottlenecks at the time of transmission (Poon et al., 2016; Varble et al., 2014; Zaraket et al., 2015) may further enhance the role of chance, as a highly adaptive variant arising in a host may not get transmitted in a particular event.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Poon et al., 2016; Varble et al., 2014; Zaraket et al., 2015

claims.claim: Selective bottlenecks could lower the barrier to emergence of human-adapted viruses.
claims.source: However, selective bottlenecks, which have been observed in experimental transmission of H5N1 and avian-like H1N1 viruses in ferrets, could lower the barrier to emergence of human-adapted viruses (Moncla et al., 2016; Wilker et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Moncla et al., 2016; Wilker et al., 2013

claims.claim: We may never isolate exactly the virus that is destined to cause a pandemic from an animal reservoir or a zoonotic human case; rather, we may isolate its evolutionary precursor.
claims.source: Even with excellent surveillance, we may never isolate exactly the virus that is destined to cause a pandemic from an animal reservoir or a zoonotic human case; rather, we may isolate its evolutionary precursor.
claims.evidence: Speculation about the limitations of surveillance

claims.claim: The most startling finding of the gain-of-transmissibility experiments with H5N1 avian influenza viruses was that so few mutations were required to convert a strain circulating in birds to mammalian transmission.
claims.source: Perhaps the most startling finding of the gain-of-transmissibility experiments with H5N1 avian influenza viruses was that so few mutations were required to convert a strain circulating in birds to mammalian transmission.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of experimental results

claims.claim: Many of the mutations identified in H5N1 gain-of-function experiments, including combinations of some of them, were already present in strains isolated during surveillance.
claims.source: This concern was reinforced by a finding that many of these mutations, including combinations of some of them, were already present in strains isolated during surveillance (Russell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Russell et al., 2012

claims.claim: The interpretation of mutations found in field strains is complicated by the problem of epistasis.
claims.source: The interpretation of the latter finding, however, is complicated by the problem of epistasis: the effect of these mutations in the genetic background of field strains may or may not be the same as in the strain studied in the laboratory.
claims.evidence: Logical reasoning about the limitations of extrapolating experimental results

claims.claim: A pandemic risk assessment informed by genetic sequence data is better than one uninformed by such sequence data.
claims.source: It seems clear that a pandemic risk assessment informed by genetic sequence data is better than one uninformed by such sequence data
claims.evidence: Logical reasoning about the value of information

claims.claim: Had the 2009 swine-origin virus been seen prior to initiating the pandemic, genetic and phenotypic considerations would have marked it as low risk, creating a false-negative risk assessment.
claims.source: We must imagine that had this strain been detected in swine surveillance prior to the pandemic emergence, genetic as well as phenotypic considerations would have marked it as low risk, creating a false-negative risk assessment.
claims.evidence: Hypothetical reasoning based on the properties of the 2009 virus

claims.claim: Whether false positive predictions of high pandemic risk are possible is more difficult to determine.
claims.source: Whether false positive predictions of high pandemic risk are also possible is more difficult to determine, because even a strain that is truly high risk may fail to cause a pandemic for any number of reasons; thus it is challenging to prove that an assessment of high risk for a particular strain was erroneous.
claims.evidence: Logical reasoning about the difficulty of evaluating predictions

claims.claim: From a decision-making perspective, a false positive is perhaps less worrisome than a false negative.
claims.source: From a decision-making perspective, a false positive is perhaps less worrisome than a false negative, as a false positive may motivate expenditure on prevention measures directed at a strain that would not have caused a pandemic, while a false negative may lead to a failure to respond to a strain that would.
claims.evidence: Reasoning about the consequences of different types of errors

claims.claim: Gain-of-transmissibility studies in highly pathogenic avian viruses have been controversial because of concerns about biosafety and biosecurity risks.
claims.source: One approach that has received considerable attention recently is to perform gain-of-transmissibility studies in highly pathogenic avian viruses; this has been controversial because of concerns about the unusual biosafety and biosecurity risks entailed in such studies (for contrasting perspectives on these risks, see the exchange in 2014–5 between Lipsitch and Inglesby, and Fouchier [Lipsitch and Inglesby, 2014, 2015; Fouchier, 2015]).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Lipsitch and Inglesby, 2014, 2015; Fouchier, 2015

claims.claim: Experiments starting from avian viruses that are not highly pathogenic in mammals can provide the same degree of causal rigor as gain-of-function in highly pathogenic avian viruses.
claims.source: One alternative is to perform similar experiments starting from avian viruses that are not highly pathogenic in mammals, and/or are related to currently circulating human seasonal viruses, so that immunity would already be present in the population. Such experiments can provide the same degree of causal rigor as gain-of-function in highly pathogenic avian viruses with novel surface antigens and can elucidate general principles of mammalian adaptation, but they cannot confirm that the same changes would be observed in other strains that are not used in the experiment.
claims.evidence: Reasoning about alternative experimental approaches

claims.claim: A recent report shows the recreation of the steps of mammalian adaptation using viruses whose HA and NA are already circulating in humans.
claims.source: A recent report shows a related way forward: the recreation of the steps of mammalian adaptation using viruses whose HA and NA are already circulating in humans (Lakdawala et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Lakdawala et al., 2015

claims.claim: A 2011 report demonstrated the importance of HA activation pH in mouse adaptation by selection experiments on a live attenuated H5N1 vaccine strain lacking the NS1 gene.
claims.source: A 2011 report employed a similar strategy, demonstrating the importance of HA activation pH in mouse adaptation by selection experiments on a live attenuated H5N1 vaccine strain lacking the NS1 gene (Krenn et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Krenn et al., 2011

claims.claim: A 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus was modified to express a mutation that increased pH of HA activation, then selected in ferrets for droplet transmission, and it was found that a second site mutation partially restored the lower pH of activation.
claims.source: More recently, a 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus was modified to express a mutation that increased pH of HA activation, then selected in ferrets for droplet transmission, and it was found that a second site mutation partially restored the lower pH of activation of the selected virus (Russier et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Russier et al., 2016

claims.claim: One limitation of de-adaptation strategies is that the acquisition of transmissibility is perhaps most likely to evolve by reversion of the de-adaptation changes.
claims.source: One limitation of de-adaptation strategies is that the acquisition of transmissibility is perhaps most likely to evolve by reversion of the de-adaptation changes.
claims.evidence: Logical reasoning about experimental design limitations

claims.claim: Epistatic effects of other loci in the genetic background of viruses used in gain-of-function and loss-of-function studies set limits to the generalizability of such experiments.
claims.source: As with all gain-of-function and loss-of-function studies, epistatic effects of other loci in the genetic background of the viruses used in such studies set limits to the generalizability of such experiments.
claims.evidence: Reasoning about limitations of experimental approaches

claims.claim: Surveillance is a key rate-limiting step for pandemic risk assessment to direct countermeasure development.
claims.source: Even if strain-based assessment methods were much better, surveillance would be a key rate-limiting step for pandemic risk assessment to direct countermeasure development.
claims.evidence: Logical reasoning about the importance of surveillance

claims.claim: We have yet to identify a pandemic strain in nonhuman hosts or in human spillover cases before the pandemic starts.
claims.source: The fact that we have yet to identify a pandemic strain in nonhuman hosts or in human spillover cases before the pandemic starts indicates there is much work to be done.
claims.evidence: Based on historical observation

claims.claim: Surveillance has expanded since the 2009 pandemic.
claims.source: Although surveillance has expanded since the 2009 pandemic, it has not been designed to optimize the chances of detecting a pandemic strain before it becomes pandemic; indeed, how to do so is not clear at present.
claims.evidence: Based on knowledge of surveillance efforts

claims.claim: Careful attention to passage histories of surveillance isolates is needed to avoid altering their genotype and phenotype post-isolation.
claims.source: The uncertainties noted above about the phenotypic characteristics of viruses isolated from previous pandemics (which may have been present in the primary isolate or may have arisen during egg passage in the laboratory) underline the need for careful attention to passage histories of surveillance isolates to avoid altering their genotype and phenotype post-isolation (Bush et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Bush et al., 2000 and logical reasoning

claims.claim: It may be improbable that we can reliably identify the 'needle in the haystack' that is the next pandemic influenza strain.
claims.source: Even with all of the foregoing suggestions in place, it may be improbable that we can reliably identify the 'needle in the haystack' that is the next pandemic influenza strain.
claims.evidence: Speculation about the limits of prediction

claims.claim: The goal is not risk assessment for its own sake, but preparedness and early response to pandemic threats.
claims.source: Ultimately, the goal is not risk assessment for its own sake, but preparedness and early response to pandemic threats.
claims.evidence: Statement of public health objectives

claims.claim: Making and improving predictions should be accompanied by a systematic effort to design responses that will not fail even if the predictions are wrong.
claims.source: In other areas where security is at stake, it has been argued that making and improving predictions should be accompanied by a systematic effort to design responses that will not fail even if the predictions are wrong (Danzig, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Danzig, 2011

claims.claim: The value of some countermeasures is strongly reliant on our ability to identify truly high-risk prepandemic threats.
claims.source: In the influenza context, the value of some countermeasures is strongly reliant on our ability to identify truly high-risk prepandemic threats: notably, preparation of seed vaccine stocks for candidate pandemic strains, stockpiling of subtype-specific vaccines, and culling of poultry infected with such strains.
claims.evidence: Reasoning about the relationship between prediction and countermeasures

claims.claim: Other types of countermeasures should provide benefits whether or not we have advance notice of the strain causing the next pandemic.
claims.source: Other types of countermeasures, ranging from strengthening local public health departments to stockpiling antivirals or ventilators to developing faster processes for vaccine manufacture to universal vaccines that should be effective against any influenza A strain, should provide benefits whether or not we have advance notice of the strain causing the next pandemic.
claims.evidence: Reasoning about robust countermeasures

claims.claim: A comprehensive assessment of priorities to prevent or mitigate the next influenza pandemic should consider the balance between improving risk assessment capacity and developing responses robust to the possibility of being caught by surprise.
claims.source: A comprehensive assessment of priorities to prevent or mitigate the next influenza pandemic should consider the balance between improving our risk assessment capacity and developing responses robust to the possibility that we will once again be caught by surprise.
claims.evidence: Recommendation based on the analysis in the review

results.result: Influenza A viruses originate in aquatic birds and sporadically transmit to terrestrial birds and mammals, where they can establish sustained circulation. This cross-species transmission involves adaptation from intestinal to respiratory tropism.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature (Krauss and Webster 2010; Vandegrift et al. 2010; Webster et al. 1992; Hinshaw et al. 1979; Hénaux and Samuel 2015). These represent foundational knowledge about influenza ecology and host adaptation.

results.result: Zoonotic influenza infections from avian and swine sources occur regularly in humans, with over 1000 cases in the last decade including H5N1, H7N9, H3N2v, H7N7, H10N8, H6N1, H9N2, and H5N6. Disease severity ranges from asymptomatic to fatal, and secondary transmission can occur.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C12 document the epidemiology of zoonotic influenza with appropriate citations for each subtype and severity range (Qin et al. 2015; Jhung et al. 2013; Fouchier et al. 2004; and others). This provides essential context for pandemic risk assessment.

results.result: Despite numerous zoonotic spillovers, only four influenza pandemics occurred in the last century. Of 18 HA and 11 NA types, only H1N1, H2N2, and H3N2 have achieved sustained human transmission, though other subtypes may have circulated before 1918.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 are supported by appropriate citations (Patterson 1986; Tong et al. 2013; Kuiken et al. 2006; Worobey et al. 2014). The rarity of pandemic emergence relative to spillover events is a key observation for understanding pandemic risk.

results.result: Multiple virus-host interactions create barriers to sustained human transmission. Ferret droplet transmission models, while imperfect, correlate with human transmissibility and have identified specific genetic changes in HA and polymerase genes required for mammalian adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 are supported by citations to Russell et al. 2014, Buhnerkempe et al. 2015, Imai et al. 2012, Herfst et al. 2012, Linster et al. 2014, Davis et al. 2014, and Schultz-Cherry et al. 2014. The ferret model's utility and limitations are appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Human infections with avian viruses show evidence of adaptive mutations (particularly PB2 627) even in first-generation zoonotic cases, indicating that host adaptation can begin immediately upon human infection. Some human infections involve incompletely adapted viruses, though interpretation is complicated by potential egg passage artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C27 are supported by multiple citations (Russell et al. 2012; Bi et al. 2015; Jonges et al. 2014; Chen et al. 2014; de Jong et al. 2006; and others). The acknowledgment of uncertainty regarding egg passage (C27) appropriately qualifies the interpretation of historical isolates.

results.result: Strain-specific countermeasures (vaccines, culling) cannot feasibly target all circulating viruses, creating value for risk assessment tools like CDC's IRAT to prioritize pandemic prevention efforts based on viral properties, epidemiology, and population attributes.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 establish the rationale for pandemic risk assessment with appropriate citations (Kaplan et al. 2016; Trock et al. 2015; Davis et al. 2014). This provides essential context for the manuscript's focus on viral trait assessment.

results.result: Pandemic prediction faces fundamental challenges: pandemics are rare events (~1 per few decades), even perfect information might only distinguish low from extremely low risk, ecological contingencies (like reassortment) are unpredictable, and intermediate evolutionary steps are difficult to observe.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37 identify key limitations in pandemic prediction with appropriate citations (King and Zeng 2001; Hansson 2006; Kucharski et al. 2015). C34 appropriately acknowledges speculation about prediction limits. These represent honest assessment of methodological challenges.

results.result: Three viral traits—HA receptor binding specificity, HA pH of activation, and polymerase complex activity—span the viral life cycle, are believed necessary for pandemic potential, typically differ between avian and mammalian-adapted viruses, and all changed during H5N1 ferret adaptation experiments. Each trait is quantitative rather than binary.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 establish the framework for the manuscript's detailed analysis. Support comes from citations (Imai et al. 2012; Linster et al. 2014), data in Tables 2-4, and Figure 1. The emphasis on quantitative nature (C42) is an important conceptual point.

results.result: Influenza HA binds sialylated glycan receptors on host cells. Avian gut and mammalian deep lung express α2,3-linked sialic acid, while mammalian upper respiratory tract (the primary site for human-adapted virus infection) expresses α2,6-linked sialic acid. Human adaptation involves switching receptor binding preference from avian to human receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C49 define receptor binding specificity with strong citation support (Russell et al. 2006; Gambaryan et al. 1997; van Riel et al. 2006; Shinya et al. 2006; Stevens et al. 2006; Chandrasekaran et al. 2008). This establishes the biological basis for the first key trait.

results.result: Error-prone influenza replication facilitates rapid emergence of HA mutations altering receptor binding. Ferret studies implicate the soft palate as an important selection site for α2,6 specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by citation to Lakdawala et al. 2015. This identifies mechanisms and anatomical sites of receptor adaptation, though generalizability beyond ferrets requires consideration.

results.result: HA structure determines receptor binding preference. Avian-adapted HAs typically have Glu190, Gln226, Gly228 (H3 numbering) and bind the trans conformation of avian receptors, while human-adapted HAs bind the cis conformation of human receptors. Specific substitutions (Gln226→Leu, Gly228→Ser in H2/H3/H5; Glu190→Asp, Gly225→Asp in H1) are associated with human adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 detail structural determinants with extensive citation support (Stevens et al. 2006; Ha et al. 2001, 2003; Gamblin et al. 2004; Liu et al. 2009; and others; Matrosovich et al. 2000; Chutinimitkul et al. 2010; Glaser et al. 2005; Tumpey et al. 2007; Koel et al. 2013). These hallmark residues are central to genetic prediction efforts.

results.result: The cis/trans definition of glycan conformation is incomplete for describing HA binding to diverse respiratory glycans. Extended conformational analysis describes overall topology and dynamics, with avian receptors adopting cone-like topology and human receptors umbrella-like topology.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 acknowledge limitations of simplified models and cite refined approaches (Chandrasekaran et al. 2008; Xu et al. 2009). This represents scientific progress in understanding receptor binding complexity.

results.result: Receptor binding assays have evolved from hemagglutination with modified erythrocytes to solid-phase assays, biosensor methods, and glycan microarrays. Microarrays allow simultaneous evaluation of binding to many sialoglycans, though current arrays may not match respiratory tract glycans.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 trace methodological development with appropriate citations (Paulson and Rogers 1987; Ito et al. 1997; Gambaryan et al. 2006, 1992; Xiong et al. 2013a; Stevens et al. 2006; Blixt et al. 2004; Childs et al. 2009; Walther et al. 2013). The limitation noted in C65 is important for interpreting array data.

results.result: Hallmark residues have substantial predictive power for receptor binding preference, correlating with adaptation in natural sequences, inducing changes when introduced experimentally, and appearing during selection experiments. However, predictions are imperfect, as evidenced by failures to switch specificity in some H5N1 backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 assess predictive value with appropriate citations (Paulson and de Vries 2013; Connor et al. 1994; Chen et al. 2012; Leigh et al. 1995; Imai et al. 2012; Tharakaraman et al. 2013). The acknowledgment of imperfection (C67) is critical for honest assessment of prediction limits.

results.result: Early pandemic viruses have shown avian or mixed receptor preference, possibly reflecting egg passage artifacts or genuine transitional evolution. An H5N1 zoonotic isolate with strong avian preference acquired human preference during ferret adaptation. Human receptor preference may indicate increased risk but is probably not necessary for pandemic initiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C73 critically evaluate receptor preference in pandemic viruses with citations (Rogers and D'Souza 1989; Connor et al. 1994; Glaser et al. 2005; Childs et al. 2009; Stevens et al. 2006, 2010; Yamada et al. 2006; Imai et al. 2012). The conclusion (C72-C73) appropriately balances risk indication against necessity, supported by Table 2 data.

results.result: After endocytosis, HA undergoes pH-triggered conformational change to fuse viral and endosomal membranes. Human-adapted viruses activate at pH 5.0-5.5; higher activation pH (typical of avian viruses) causes premature inactivation in the mildly acidic mammalian respiratory tract. Lower activation pH indicates greater human adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C79 define HA pH of activation with citations (Di Lella et al. 2016; Zaraket et al. 2013a) and established knowledge of cellular biology and influenza entry. This establishes the biological basis for the second key trait.

results.result: During endocytosis, virions encounter progressively lower pH in early endosomes (6.0-6.5), late endosomes (5.0-5.5), and lysosomes (4.6-5.0). Excessive HA stability prevents fusion in endosomes, leading to lysosomal degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 describe the endocytic pathway with appropriate citations (Mellman et al. 1986; Skehel and Wiley 2000). This explains the functional constraints on HA activation pH.

results.result: Human-transmissible viruses have more acid-stable HA (lower activation pH) than avian viruses. Human seasonal H1N1, H2N2, H3N2 activate at pH 5.0-5.4; 2009 pandemic H1N1 initially at pH 5.5, later evolving to 5.2-5.4. Avian viruses range from pH 4.6-6.0, with low-pathogenic duck viruses at 5.3-6.0 and highly pathogenic at 5.6-6.0.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87 characterize activation pH ranges with strong citation support (Russell 2014; Galloway et al. 2013; Cotter et al. 2014; Maurer-Stroh et al. 2010; Russier et al. 2016; Scholtissek 1985). This provides empirical basis for distinguishing human and avian adaptation.

results.result: In H5N1 viruses, higher activation pH (5.2-6.0 range) associates with increased replication and pathogenicity in chickens. Conversely, decreasing activation pH from 5.9 to 5.4 attenuates growth and prevents transmission in ducks but increases growth in mammalian upper respiratory tracts.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 demonstrate host-specific fitness effects with appropriate citations (DuBois et al. 2011; Reed et al. 2009; Zaraket et al. 2013a, 2013b). This supports the concept of divergent selection pressures in different hosts.

results.result: In ferret adaptation experiments, H5N1 viruses required decreased HA activation pH for airborne transmissibility, following receptor-binding switch and glycosylation changes. However, acid stability change alone is insufficient without human receptor-binding specificity. HA activation pH ≤5.5 was required for 2009 H1N1 pandemic potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 synthesize ferret adaptation findings with citations (Imai et al. 2012; Herfst et al. 2012; Zaraket et al. 2013a; Shelton et al. 2013; Russier et al. 2016). This demonstrates that pH adaptation is necessary but not sufficient, requiring coordination with other traits.

results.result: Nearly 100 mutations alter HA activation pH across influenza subtypes. These residues are distributed throughout HA1 and HA2 in regions undergoing structural changes during refolding, but don't alter prefusion structure. NA and M proteins can also modulate HA stability in some cases.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 characterize genetic determinants with appropriate citations (Russell 2014; Mair et al. 2014; Bullough et al. 1994; Wilson et al. 1981; DuBois et al. 2011; Weis et al. 1990; de Vries et al. 2014; Huang et al. 1980; Su et al. 2009; Reed et al. 2010; O'Donnell et al. 2014). The complexity noted complicates genetic prediction.

results.result: Early 2009 H1N1pdm had intermediate activation pH (5.5), with subsequent isolates evolving to 5.2-5.4, suggesting pH 5.5 may be the upper limit for pandemic potential. Destabilizing mutations cause loss of ferret transmissibility, restored by mutations lowering pH to 5.3.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 analyze 2009 pandemic evolution with citation support (Russier et al. 2016). This provides evidence that even pandemic viruses may not initially have optimal human adaptation and can evolve post-emergence.

results.result: While HA activation pH suitable for human infection is typical of pandemic and seasonal influenza (Table 3), humans can have symptomatic infection with viruses having activation pH in the terrestrial bird range. Conversely, some avian H9, H10, H14, H15 isolates display human-typical activation pH.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 acknowledge exceptions to general patterns, supported by Galloway et al. 2013 and Table 3 data. This demonstrates that pH adaptation alone is insufficient for pandemic risk assessment, consistent with the multi-trait framework.

results.result: The influenza polymerase complex (PA, PB1, PB2) and nucleoprotein are required for genome transcription and replication. Avian virus polymerase genes differ genetically from human virus counterparts and perform inefficiently in human cells. Efficient polymerase activity in human cells is required for human-to-human transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C108 define polymerase complex efficiency with appropriate citations (Huang et al. 1990; Chen et al. 2006; Cauldwell et al. 2014; Naffakh et al. 2008). This establishes the biological basis for the third key trait.

results.result: PB2 mutations are consistently associated with mammalian polymerase function. PB2 residue 627 (Glu in avian, Lys in human-adapted viruses including 1918, 1957, 1968 pandemics) was identified in 1977. The 2009 pandemic virus is an exception, having acquired mammalian adaptation through different PB2 mutations (271, 590, 591) after avian PB2 introduction into swine in the 1990s.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C114 trace the history of polymerase adaptation research with citations (Spooner and Barry 1977; Subbarao et al. 1993; Mehle and Doudna 2009) and Figure 2. The 2009 exception (C112-C114) is critical for understanding prediction limitations.

results.result: PB2 residues 627, 271, 590, and 591 lie on the same external surface. Mammalian-adapting mutations increase positive charge, suggesting interaction with enhancing host factors or repulsion of restriction factors. ANP32A, differing between mammals and flighted birds, is a polymerase cofactor explaining inefficient avian polymerase function and selection for 627Glu→Lys in mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 integrate structural and mechanistic understanding with citations (Mehle and Doudna 2009; Long et al. 2016). The ANP32A discovery (C117) represents major progress in understanding host-specific polymerase function.

results.result: PB2 residue 701 is implicated in mammalian adaptation. Mutations at 701, 702, and 714 affect PB2-importin-alpha interactions, potentially enhancing nuclear import or affecting polymerase function in the nucleus.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 identify additional adaptation sites with citations (Resa-Infante et al. 2008; Gabriel et al. 2005; Sediri et al. 2015). This demonstrates multiple pathways to polymerase adaptation.

results.result: PB2 adaptive mutations emerge during mammalian infection, observed in fatal H7N7 human cases, mouse passage experiments, and associated with greater severity in H7N9 and H5N1 zoonotic cases. However, some avian strains may be less able to accept these mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C125 document adaptive evolution with appropriate citations (Jonges et al. 2014; de Jong et al. 2013, 2006; Sha et al. 2016; Long et al. 2013). This demonstrates real-time adaptation during infection and strain-specific constraints.

results.result: Nuclear export protein (NEP) plays an important role in polymerase function, regulating transcription-replication balance. In H5N1 isolates lacking PB2 adaptations, NEP mutations can compensate for inefficient avian polymerase in human cells. However, NEP overexpression inhibits human-adapted polymerase. The minimal polymerase assay is insufficient to predict functional adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C130 identify NEP's compensatory role with citations (Robb et al. 2009; Mänz et al. 2012; Chua et al. 2013; Paterson and Fodor 2012; Robb and Fodor 2012). The conclusion (C130) appropriately identifies assay limitations.

results.result: Many circulating H5N1 viruses already have PB2 627K or 701N mutations (likely from reintroduction of mammalian-adapted strains), associated with more severe human cases. However, these strains haven't achieved sustained human transmission, demonstrating polymerase adaptation is necessary but not sufficient. The 2009 pandemic's lack of 627K demonstrates limitations of single-mutation prediction.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C134 synthesize observations about necessity versus sufficiency with citations (Long et al. 2013; de Jong et al. 2006; Herfst et al. 2010). This is a critical conclusion for pandemic risk assessment, supported by Table 4 data.

results.result: No single polymerase mutation predicts pandemic risk for all viruses, but the concept that polymerase must adapt to human cells before extensive human-to-human transmission is consistent with the four modern pandemic jumps.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 provide balanced conclusions about polymerase adaptation. While no single mutation is universally predictive, the general principle of required adaptation is supported by pandemic history. This appropriately acknowledges both limitations and general principles.

results.result: Despite tremendous progress in understanding viral adaptation traits and their genetic basis, sequence data must be considered alongside experimental and epidemiological data. The 2013 Cambodian H5N1 outbreak, where viruses contained human-adaptive mutations, led to vaccine candidate production.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C141 provide context for integrated risk assessment with citation (Davis et al. 2014). The Cambodia example illustrates practical application of genetic surveillance, though the outcome (no pandemic) also illustrates prediction challenges.

results.result: Sequence-based phenotype predictions are not infallible due to: (1) large numbers of sites involved in determining traits, (2) important role of epistasis, and (3) imperfect sequence-to-trait mapping. Hallmark HA residues don't always change specificity depending on background. The 2009 pandemic virus had avian-adapted PB2 627/701 residues; introducing human-adapted residues didn't improve replication. Other PB2 sites were later identified as responsible for adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C148 critically assess prediction limitations with extensive citations (Raman et al. 2014; Russell et al. 2014; Kryazhimskiy et al. 2011; Gong and Bloom 2014; and others; Herfst et al. 2010; Jagger et al. 2010; Mehle and Doudna 2009; Yamada et al. 2010). The 2009 example powerfully illustrates epistasis and the danger of relying on known markers.

results.result: All three traits (receptor binding, pH activation, polymerase efficiency) must be present to some degree for pandemic potential. With few pandemic instances per century, new strains may violate apparent adaptation rules (as with 2009 PB2 and pH). Whether the trait list is complete is unclear. Full human adaptation may not be required for pandemic initiation. Failure to fully meet criteria doesn't disqualify pandemic risk.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C153 synthesize key conclusions with appropriate citations (Russier et al. 2016; Childs et al. 2009). The acknowledgment of uncertainty (C151) and incomplete adaptation (C152-C153) are critical for honest risk assessment. These claims are well-supported by the evidence presented throughout, particularly Tables 2-3.

results.result: Even perfectly adapted viruses might fail to transmit extensively due to ecological factors or chance. Pandemic initiation requires viral adaptation plus ecological opportunity for spillover, immunologically susceptible populations, and sufficient connectivity. Within-host and transmission selection pressures may diverge. Genetic bottlenecks enhance chance, while selective bottlenecks could lower emergence barriers.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C158 acknowledge non-viral factors in pandemic emergence with citations (Mills et al. 2006; Park et al. 2013; Poon et al. 2016; Varble et al. 2014; Zaraket et al. 2015; Moncla et al. 2016; Wilker et al. 2013). This appropriately broadens risk assessment beyond viral traits alone.

results.result: Surveillance may only detect evolutionary precursors, not the actual pandemic strain. H5N1 gain-of-function experiments showed few mutations were required for mammalian transmission, and many identified mutations (including combinations) were already present in surveillance strains. However, epistasis complicates interpretation since mutation effects may differ across genetic backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C162 discuss surveillance limitations and gain-of-function findings with citation (Russell et al. 2012). C159 is appropriately speculative. The epistasis caveat (C162) is critical for interpreting surveillance data.

results.result: Sequence-informed risk assessment is better than uninformed assessment, but the 2009 virus would likely have been marked low risk based on pre-pandemic knowledge (intermediate receptor binding, high activation pH, avian-adapted PB2), creating a false negative. False positives are harder to prove since high-risk strains may fail to cause pandemics for other reasons. False negatives are more concerning than false positives from a decision-making perspective.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C166 provide honest assessment of prediction value and limitations. The 2009 counterfactual (C164) is speculative but well-reasoned based on the virus's properties. The risk asymmetry argument (C166) is logically sound for public health decision-making.

results.result: Gain-of-transmissibility studies in highly pathogenic avian viruses are controversial due to biosafety/biosecurity concerns. Alternatives include experiments with non-highly pathogenic viruses or those related to circulating human strains, which provide similar causal rigor for general principles but cannot confirm findings apply to other strains. Recent studies recreate mammalian adaptation using viruses with HA/NA already circulating in humans or attenuated vaccine strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C171 discuss experimental approaches with citations (Lipsitch and Inglesby 2014, 2015; Fouchier 2015; Lakdawala et al. 2015; Krenn et al. 2011; Russier et al. 2016). The acknowledgment of controversy and presentation of alternatives is balanced. Limitations of alternatives are appropriately noted.

results.result: De-adaptation strategies have the limitation that transmissibility acquisition may most likely evolve by reverting the de-adaptation changes. Epistatic effects in genetic backgrounds limit generalizability of all gain/loss-of-function studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C173 identify experimental limitations through logical reasoning. These are valid methodological concerns that appropriately qualify the interpretation of such experiments.

results.result: Surveillance is a key rate-limiting step for risk assessment. No pandemic strain has been identified in non-human hosts or spillover cases before pandemic onset. Although surveillance has expanded since 2009, it hasn't been designed to optimize pre-pandemic detection. Careful attention to passage histories is needed to avoid post-isolation genotype/phenotype alterations.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C177 identify surveillance challenges with citation (Bush et al. 2000). C175 is a critical observation about surveillance limitations. The passage history concern (C177) is well-founded given uncertainties about historical isolates noted earlier.

results.result: Reliably identifying the next pandemic strain may be improbable. The goal is preparedness and early response, not risk assessment per se. Predictions should be accompanied by responses robust to prediction failure. Some countermeasures (seed stocks, subtype-specific vaccines, culling) rely on identifying high-risk threats, while others (public health infrastructure, antivirals, faster manufacturing, universal vaccines) provide benefits regardless of advance notice. Comprehensive pandemic priorities should balance improving risk assessment with developing robust responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C183 provide strategic recommendations with citation (Danzig 2011). C178 is appropriately speculative. The distinction between prediction-dependent and prediction-independent countermeasures (C181-C182) is important for policy. The final recommendation (C183) appropriately balances different approaches.
